characters: Kwaku: an eleven-year-old Ghanaian boy in Primary 6, wearing a neat cream-and-brown school uniform and carrying a history notebook.
Abena: his thirteen-year-old sister in JHS 1, braided hair tied neatly, wearing the same cream-and-brown uniform.
Curator Agyeman: a knowledgeable Ghanaian museum historian at Manhyia Palace Museum in Kumasi, wearing a rich kente scarf over a black suit jacket and glasses.
Historical portrayal (in museum paintings and exhibits): Nana Yaa Asantewaa, Queen Mother of Ejisu (born c. 1840s), dignified elder leader in traditional battle smock (batakari) and kente.

narrationPlan.voice: Dignified, warm Ghanaian English storyteller (`Kore`) for Upper Primary and JHS 1.
notes: Use phonetic hints for Asantewaa, Ejisu, Prempeh, Manhyia, Kumasi, Kwaku, and Abena while keeping standard written spellings.

music: Optional solemn fontomfrom and kora historical underscore, off by default.
culturalNotes: Strictly separates verified historical facts and oral-tradition summaries from invented verbatim dialogue.
reviewQuestions: Confirm with an Ashanti history reviewer whether both "Ejisu" and "Edweso" should be noted in classroom materials.

pages.brief: Courtyard and gallery of Manhyia Palace Museum in Kumasi. Kwaku (11, cream-and-brown uniform, notebook) and Abena (13, same uniform) standing with Curator Agyeman (glasses, kente scarf over dark jacket) beside a dignified bronze statue of Nana Yaa Asantewaa.
pages.narration: Respectful, engaging opening. Clear pronunciation of "Manhyia", "Kumasi", "Asantewaa", and "Ejisu".

pages.brief: Inside the museum gallery: Curator Agyeman pointing to sepia historical photographs and bound archival ledgers inside a glass display case (no readable text) while Kwaku and Abena look closely.
pages.narration: Clear, thoughtful explanation of historical evidence versus invented quotes.

pages.brief: Warmly lit museum painting showing Nana Yaa Asantewaa dressed in traditional kente seated in a courtyard at Ejisu, listening to and advising elders with calm dignity.
pages.narration: Steady, respectful tone explaining the constitutional role of the Queen Mother.

pages.brief: Museum wall map of Africa and the Indian Ocean (no text labels) with a glowing line tracing the sea journey from the Gold Coast to Sierra Leone and the Seychelles, watched by Abena and Kwaku.
pages.narration: Sombre and clear. Emphasise the year "eighteen ninety-six" and "Nana Prempeh the First".

pages.brief: Respectful museum illustration showing the sacred Golden Stool resting upon its own raised ceremonial chair and embroidered cushion, surrounded by attendants under royal umbrellas.
pages.narration: Reverent and clear: "never sat upon by anyone" and "represents the soul, unity and living spirit".

pages.brief: Historical museum panel depicting the outdoor durbar at Kumasi in March 1900: British colonial officials on a veranda facing rows of dignified Asante chiefs seated under umbrellas in solemn silence.
Warm lamplit historical scene: Nana Yaa Asantewaa standing tall and resolute in the centre of a council of seated Asante elders at night, her hand raised in a gesture of firm resolve.
pages.narration: Quiet tension building to Yaa Asantewaa’s moment of leadership.

pages.brief: Curator Agyeman speaking to Kwaku and Abena beside a museum display showing Nana Yaa Asantewaa inspiring the council of chiefs.
pages.narration: Honest historical framing ("historians do not claim a word-for-word transcript") paired with inspiring delivery of her recorded message.

pages.brief: Dignified museum portrait of Nana Yaa Asantewaa wearing a traditional woven batakari smock, holding a ceremonial staff as she consults calmly with Asante leaders in the forest (non-graphic, no violence).
pages.narration: Strong, respectful cadence highlighting her strategic leadership at age sixty.

pages.brief: Kwaku and Abena looking respectfully at a framed sepia portrait on the museum wall showing elderly Asante royals seated with quiet dignity during their exile in the Seychelles.
Inside the bright museum hall, Curator Agyeman smiling as Kwaku writes in his notebook and Abena looks up with pride.
pages.narration: Triumphant clarity on "Never! ... the Golden Stool was kept hidden and safe".

pages.brief: Sunny courtyard of Manhyia Palace Museum: Kwaku and Abena smiling and waving goodbye to Curator Agyeman near the museum gardens.
pages.narration: Inspiring, thoughtful conclusion. Gentle pause before "The end".

teacherGuide.overview: Framed through a guided visit to the Manhyia Palace Museum in Kumasi, this Primary 5–JHS 1 story presents the verified historical context of Nana Yaa Asantewaa (Queen Mother of Ejisu), the 1896 exile of Asantehene Nana Prempeh I, the sacred meaning of the Golden Stool (Sika Dwa Kofi), Governor Frederick Hodgson’s demand on 28 March 1900, and the 1900 War of the Golden Stool, while explicitly teaching learners how historians distinguish primary records and oral traditions from invented dialogue.
learningGoals: Explain the constitutional role of the Queen Mother (Ohemmaa) in Asante governance and identify Nana Yaa Asantewaa as Queen Mother of Ejisu.
Explain why the Golden Stool (Sika Dwa Kofi) is sacred to the Asante nation and why Governor Hodgson’s demand on 28 March 1900 provoked resistance.
Distinguish between verified historical facts, oral traditions of speeches, and modern museum framing.
Reflect on how courage, sacrifice, and unity protect national dignity.

beforeReading: Locate Kumasi and Ejisu in the Ashanti Region on a map of Ghana, and locate Sierra Leone and the Seychelles on a map of Africa and the Indian Ocean.
Ask learners: "How do we know what happened in Ghana before anyone now living was born?"
whileReading: Pause after page 2 to discuss why historians cross-check multiple sources (written dispatches, photos, and oral traditions).
Pause after page 8 to note why Curator Agyeman explains that Yaa Asantewaa’s speech is preserved in meaning through oral history rather than a tape recording.
afterReading: Create a two-column chart on the board: "Verified Historical Facts (with dates)" and "Lessons on Leadership for Today".
discussion: Why was the Golden Stool never sat upon, and why did Governor Hodgson’s demand show a deep misunderstanding of Asante culture and sovereignty?
What role did women play in leadership and governance in traditional Ghanaian societies as shown by Nana Yaa Asantewaa?
Even though Nana Yaa Asantewaa was eventually captured and exiled to the Seychelles, why do historians consider the defence of the Golden Stool a lasting triumph?
reflection: When is a time in school or community life when standing up for what is right requires quiet courage?

mathsExtension.task: Nana Prempeh I was exiled in 1896 and returned to Kumasi in 1924. How many years was he in exile?
The War of the Golden Stool began in March 1900 and Nana Yaa Asantewaa passed away in the Seychelles in 1921. How many years passed between March 1900 and 1921?

support: Use a visual timeline with four dates: 1896 (Exile of Prempeh I), 28 March 1900 (Hodgson’s demand & Yaa Asantewaa’s leadership), 1921 (Yaa Asantewaa’s passing in Seychelles), and 1924 (Return of Prempeh I).
stretch: Write a short historical essay explaining how comparing British colonial records and Asante oral traditions gives a fuller picture of the 1900 war than reading only one side.

culturalNotes: Nana Yaa Asantewaa (c. 1840–1921) was the Edwesohemmaa (Queen Mother of Ejisu/Edweso). Manhyia Palace Museum in Kumasi preserves royal Asante history and artefacts.
localiseThis: Connect to respected historical leaders (male and female) from your own region or traditional area in Ghana.

whatWeKnow: In 1896 British authorities exiled Asantehene Nana Prempeh I; on 28 March 1900 Governor Sir Frederick Hodgson demanded the Golden Stool at Kumasi.

Nana Yaa Asantewaa, Queen Mother of Ejisu, led the 1900 resistance (War of the Golden Stool); she was later exiled to the Seychelles where she died in October 1921, while the Golden Stool was never captured.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: Ghanaian and international historians continue archiving local family oral histories, photographs from the Seychelles exile, and regional accounts of the 1900 stockade defences across Ashanti towns.

investigation.title: Be a Historian: Compare Two Eyewitness Accounts
materials: A short 1-minute classroom action (for example, the teacher walks to the board, draws a star, puts down the chalk, and opens a window)
steps: Have the teacher perform a short 4-step action in front of the class without announcing it beforehand.
Ask three learners sitting in different parts of the room to write down what they saw, and ask a fourth learner to interview them and combine the evidence.
Compare the accounts: which details did every witness agree on, and which details were only visible from one angle?
investigation.whatToNotice: Different witnesses notice different details, so historians compare multiple independent accounts and physical clues to reconstruct what truly happened!
investigation.safetyNote: Standard classroom activity; treat every classmate’s written observation respectfully.

factCheck.claim: On 28 March 1900, British Governor Sir Frederick Hodgson demanded the Golden Stool in Kumasi, and Nana Yaa Asantewaa (Queen Mother of Ejisu) led the subsequent resistance.
factCheck.explanation: Hodgson’s demand is documented in British Colonial Office dispatches (Gold Coast Confidential, 1900), and Yaa Asantewaa’s leadership of the 1900 uprising and subsequent exile to the Seychelles (d. 17 October 1921) are established in Ghanaian and imperial historiography.
factCheck.reference: Boahen, A. A. (2003). Yaa Asantewaa and the Asante-British War of 1900–1. James Currey / Sub-Saharan Publishers; Arhin, K. (2000). The Role of Yaa Asantewaa in the 1900 Asante War of Resistance; Manhyia Palace Museum Historical Archives.

reviewerNotes: HIGH RISK: "nhy" cluster needs native-speaker demonstration.

pronunciation.guidance: a single long "YAAH" (the double a marks a long vowel).
reviewerNotes: Confirm vowel length; engines may shorten it to "ya".
Confirm stress and final long vowel.
Confirm local Twi pronunciation (Edweso vs Ejisu).
Confirm the vowel in the first syllable (oh vs aw).
